## Overview

### 1. Epidemiological Inflection in 2026: The CRE Threat Recalibrated

The year 2026 constitutes a decisive inflection point in the global trajectory of carbapenem-resistant Enterobacteriaceae (CRE). Preliminary data from the 2025 survey of carbapenem-resistant Enterobacterales (CRE25), reported to the EU/EEA on 29 June 2026, document a fundamental shift in the molecular epidemiology of the resistance threat: a marked contraction in the proportion of *bla*<sub>KPC</sub> carbapenemase genes alongside a corresponding expansion of *bla*<sub>NDM</sub>-bearing isolates within *Klebsiella pneumoniae* species complex (SC) and *Escherichia coli* [12]. This redistribution is not incidental—it is driven by the acquisition of *bla*<sub>NDM</sub> by previously circulating high-risk lineages (notably sequence type ST147) and the de novo emergence of novel high-risk lineages (ST383, ST395), a finding consistent with the European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control's (ECDC) third update on carbapenem-resistant Enterobacterales, which had already warned of "concerning changes... including the increased acquisition of carbapenemase genes by high-risk lineages" [7]. The European Commission's Health Security Committee, in its formal Opinion of 13 May 2025, elevated the issue to a cross-border health security priority, citing the "rapidly increasing incidence of carbapenem-resistant Enterobacterales (CRE) in healthcare settings" [9]. Against this backdrop, a comprehensive assessment of (i) the quantitative dynamics of resistance dissemination, (ii) attributable mortality, and (iii) the comparative clinical and economic performance of next-generation β-lactam/β-lactamase inhibitor (BLI) regimens versus bacteriophage (phage) therapy is both timely and scientifically mandatory. This report addresses that mandate.
